w: What's tested hCG: made by the trophoblasts, it rescues the corpus luteum ("this is the important part... this is what rescues the corpus luteum"), keeps progesterone and estrogen high and LH and FSH low, and is what a pregnancy test measures; the corpus luteum carries the first trimester, then the placenta takes over Lactation: prolactin makes the milk and oxytocin lets it down; during pregnancy progesterone holds prolactin back ("what you should know"); dopamine tonically inhibits prolactin, suckling turns it down, and prolactin inhibits GnRH ("one thing that I want to highlight") Fertilization: ZP3 sets off the acrosomal reaction ("one of those proteins that's really important"), then ZP2, the second meiotic division and the cortical reaction that blocks polyspermy; capacitation has to come first The pregnancy steroids ("the main hormones that I care more about"): estriol is the estrogen of pregnancy; the placenta makes progesterone on its own but needs the fetus's 17,20 desmolase to make estrogen Implantation (trophoblasts, cytotrophoblasts versus syncytiotrophoblasts, decidualization) and the placenta's other hormones: human placental lactogen opposes insulin, and relaxin keeps the uterus quiet Labor: a rising estrogen-to-progesterone ratio, prostaglandins and oxytocin from the posterior pituitary, which also limits bleeding after delivery; and the endocrine basis of contraception 1 hCG rescues the corpus luteum: made by the trophoblasts, it keeps the corpus luteum making progesterone (the hormone that readies the endometrium) and estrogen through the first trimester, LH and FSH stay suppressed, and it is what a pregnancy test measures Study guide + recording · 6 questions in the bank Know this A pregnancy test detects hCG, found in urine or blood about 10 to 11 days after fertilization. hCG is also what a pregnancy test measures: "it's very high, very quickly." His slide notes add that it can be found in urine or blood about 10 to 11 days after fertilization, and that it is highest toward the end of the first trimester, at about 10 weeks, then declines for the rest of pregnancy. 2 Prolactin versus oxytocin: prolactin makes the milk and oxytocin lets it down through the myoepithelial cells; during pregnancy progesterone antagonizes prolactin, so full milk production waits for delivery Study guide + recording · 3 questions in the bank Know this Prolactin makes the milk; oxytocin contracts the myoepithelial cells to let it down. Once the baby and placenta are delivered, progesterone falls, and prolactin's brake comes off. Prolactin then drives full milk production in the alveoli. Around each alveolus are myoepithelial cells, which respond to oxytocin by contracting, and that squeezes the milk out: milk letdown. "Prolactin sets the stage and creates all the milk products. Oxytocin is going to stimulate milk letdown." 3 Suckling's neuroendocrine effects: dopamine tonically inhibits prolactin; suckling lowers dopamine and raises oxytocin from the posterior pituitary; prolactin inhibits GnRH, so periods stop Study guide + recording · 3 questions in the bank Know this Dr. Herr's Exam 3 study guide (no in-class review this time). It points at the second half of Dr. Madison's lecture: hCG keeping the corpus luteum making progesterone until the placenta takes over; the labor hormones, and oxytocin clamping the uterus after delivery while the fall in placental progesterone frees prolactin to make milk; prolactin makes the milk and oxytocin lets it down; suckling lowers dopamine (so prolactin rises), releases oxytocin, and the prolactin holds GnRH down. The guide doesn't list fertilization, implantation or capacitation; they stay in the hub, ranked after these. High prolactin inhibits GnRH, so LH, FSH and the sex steroids fall: the amenorrhea of breastfeeding and of hyperprolactinemia. "One thing that I want to highlight": prolactin inhibits GnRH, gonadotropin-releasing hormone. Less GnRH means less LH and FSH and lower sex steroids downstream, which is why high prolactin brings amenorrhea. It is the same mechanism as hyperprolactinemia, high prolactin from any cause, and it is why a breastfeeding mother's periods often stop. On this slide, he said, "mainly focus on this side of things. Dopamine being important." Estrogen increases uterine contractility and progesterone relaxes the myometrium, so as the ratio of estrogen to progesterone rises late in pregnancy, around 40 weeks, the myometrium shifts to a contracting state. Increased uterine production of prostaglandins, PGE2 and PGF2 alpha. They raise intracellular calcium, and calcium drives muscle contraction, so contractions get stronger and more rhythmic. Prostaglandins also soften and thin the cervix; he singled out PGE2 for the softening. 5 The placenta takes over the steroids: estriol is the estrogen of pregnancy; the placenta makes progesterone on its own but needs the fetal adrenal's 17,20 desmolase and the fetal liver before its aromatase makes estriol Study guide + recording · 3 questions in the bank Because estriol needs a working fetal adrenal and liver, the mother's estriol level reflects the health of the fetus. The placenta can also use DHEA sulfate to make estradiol. The take-home, in his slide notes: to make estrogen, the placenta "needs help from the baby." 6 Human placental lactogen opposes insulin: an insulin-resistant, hyperinsulinemic pregnancy and gestational diabetes Study guide + recording · 3 questions in the bank That is part of why pregnancy is an insulin-resistant, hyperinsulinemic state: the mother's tissues respond less to insulin, she uses more fat and spares glucose, and her insulin levels can run very high. Some mothers develop gestational diabetes. He called it multifactorial. Much of it is hormonal, since several placental and pregnancy hormones oppose insulin, but some women have a higher genetic predisposition, and no single hormone drives it. hPL is the one with research interest. 7 What the placenta makes: hCG, hPL, relaxin, progesterone and estriol, but not oxytocin Study guide + slides · 1 question in the bank Suckling also makes the hypothalamus produce oxytocin, which is carried to the posterior pituitary and released into the blood to reach the breast. 8 Building the breast for milk: estrogen grows and branches the ducts, progesterone adds the alveoli, prolactin and cortisol raise the milk enzymes Study guide + recording · 2 questions in the bank Estrogen: ductal and lobular growth and ductal branching, and more fat deposition in the breast. The cortical reaction, also called the zonal reaction: the oocyte releases its cortical granules, and the remaining zona proteins are shed, so no other sperm can bind. That prevents polyspermy, fertilization by more than one sperm. A single sperm fertilizes a single egg. ZP3 First, on reaching the zona pellucida The acrosomal reaction: enzymes digest the zona, and the ZP3 layer is cleaved away ZP2 After the acrosomal reaction, once ZP3 is gone The oocyte's second meiotic division, and the cortical (zonal) reaction that blocks polyspermy 11 Implantation at the blastocyst stage: trophoblasts, cytotrophoblasts (nurse cells) versus syncytiotrophoblasts (invasion) Recording + objectives · 2 questions in the bank Attachment, or adhesion. Adhesion molecules on the trophoblasts and on the endometrial cells bind the blastocyst firmly to the wall. He named L-selectin as one but said, "I don't care that you know them." The important thing is that attachment signals the trophoblasts to differentiate into two populations: cytotrophoblasts, the nurse cells that nourish the early embryo and give it structure, and syncytiotrophoblasts, the invaders. Also flagged in class ZP3 on the zona pellucida sets off the acrosomal reaction; after it, the sperm binds ZP2. The trophoblasts start secreting hCG about 8 days after ovulation, and it keeps the corpus luteum from regressing. His summary of hCG's two jobs: the corpus luteum stays alive and keeps making progesterone and estrogen, and LH and FSH stay low. First trimester: the corpus luteum makes most of the progesterone and estrogen; after it, the placenta takes over. Know where the pregnancy steroids come from: the placenta makes progesterone on its own and estriol only with the fetus's 17,20 desmolase. Estradiol is the cycle's estrogen, estrone menopause's, and estriol pregnancy's. Oxytocin from the posterior pituitary drives labor's contractions, and after delivery the continuing contractions limit bleeding. Progesterone antagonizes prolactin in the breast during pregnancy, so full milk production waits until progesterone falls after delivery. On the prolactin and oxytocin slide, focus on the hypothalamus: dopamine tonically inhibits prolactin release, and suckling turns the dopamine down. You can skip Skip the names of the cleavage stages; know that implantation happens at the blastocyst stage and that trophoblasts form its outer layer. Know that adhesion molecules attach the blastocyst and signal the trophoblasts to differentiate, not the molecules' names. He skipped the methods that keep sperm and egg apart; know the endocrine ones: the pill blunts the LH surge, progestin thickens mucus, high-dose estrogen prevents implantation.
